content: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells, representing approximately 1% of all cancers and 12% of hematological malignancies. Bortezomib, the first proteasome inhibitor of its kind, is widely used in the treatment of both newly diagnosed and relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. It can be administered as a single agent or in combination with other therapies. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to evaluate the effects of bortezomib on overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), response rate (RR), health-related quality of life (HRQoL), adverse events (AEs), and treatment-related death (TRD). The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing bortezomib to no bortezomib, either with the same or different background therapies, as well as trials comparing different doses, administration methods, and schedules of bortezomib. The search for relevant studies included databases such as MEDLINE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and EMBASE, as well as conference proceedings and clinical trial registries, up to January 27, 2016. A total of 3,667 records were screened, and 16 RCTs involving 5,626 patients were identified, with 12 trials included in the meta-analyses. All trials were randomized and open-label, though two were only available in abstract form, limiting the ability to fully assess the risk of bias. Moderate-quality evidence from four studies (1,586 patients) demonstrated that bortezomib significantly improves OS (Peto OR 0.77, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.92) when compared to no bortezomib with the same background therapy. Similarly, moderate-quality evidence from five studies (1,855 patients) showed that bortezomib improves PFS (Peto OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.74) in this comparison. High-quality evidence from five studies (2,532 patients) indicated that bortezomib improves OS (Peto OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.88) when compared to no bortezomib with different background therapies or other agents. However, evidence for PFS in this comparison was of low quality (four studies, 2,489 patients; Peto OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.75). Four trials (716 patients) examined different doses, administration methods, and treatment schedules of bortezomib, but these were reviewed qualitatively rather than quantitatively. Time to progression (TTP) was assessed in four trials, and PFS data were extracted and analyzed for three of these studies. In one study, TTP data were used as a proxy for PFS due to the unavailability of PFS data. TTP was not analyzed separately in this review. Patients receiving bortezomib were found to have an increased risk of several adverse events, including thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, gastrointestinal toxicities, peripheral neuropathy, infections, and fatigue. The quality of evidence for these risks varied. High-quality evidence indicated an increased risk of cardiac disorders in patients treated with bortezomib compared to those not receiving it, particularly in trials with different background therapies or other agents. The risk of treatment-related death (TRD) was uncertain due to low-quality evidence. Only four trials assessed HRQoL, and the data were insufficient for meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses by disease setting showed improvements in all outcomes with bortezomib. In terms of therapy setting, bortezomib demonstrated benefits across all outcomes and subgroups, except for OS following consolidation therapy. In conclusion, this meta-analysis found that bortezomib provides significant benefits in terms of OS, PFS, and response rate for patients with multiple myeloma compared to those not receiving bortezomib. These benefits were observed regardless of whether the background therapy was the same or different, or whether bortezomib was compared to other agents. Further research is needed to evaluate newer proteasome inhibitors to determine if they offer a better risk-benefit profile. Additionally, more studies are required to assess the impact of bortezomib on HRQoL.
